title: Yom Kippur: Jonah
hookLine: the afternoon reads Jonah, and the whole city of Nineveh turns

cards: It's three or four in the afternoon. The fast is nearly a day old. Heads ache.
Somebody's dozing in the back row. And at the afternoon service, the reader chants the whole book of Jonah: four short chapters.

A prophet runs away from God, gets thrown off a ship in a storm, spends three days inside a great fish, and finally goes where he was sent. The fish is what sticks. But the reason to read it today comes after the fish.

teach.b: Jonah is sent to Nineveh, that great city, the capital of Israel's enemy. He runs. Later he says why: he knew God was gracious and would relent, and he didn't want the city spared.
When he finally arrives, his whole sermon is five Hebrew words: yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. And then, astonishingly, it works. The people of Nineveh believe.
They fast. Everyone puts on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king gets up from his throne, sits in ashes, and orders even the animals to fast.
Then the line: "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, which He said He would do unto them; and He did it not."
The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, points out what that verse doesn't say. It doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says God saw their works: their deeds changed.
That's a sharp message for a room full of people fasting right now. The fast alone, the Mishnah suggests, isn't what's seen; what changes afterward is.

The book ends with Jonah angry outside the city, and God asking him about mercy: should I not have pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, "and also much cattle?"

teach.h: A BOOK THAT ENDS ON A QUESTION.
teach.b: The book ends on that question, without Jonah's answer.
If even Nineveh can turn, the reasoning goes, so can anyone in this room.

how: At the afternoon (Mincha) service of Yom Kippur, the entire book of Jonah is chanted as the haftarah, followed by verses from Micah in many communities.

games.q: you're the king of Nineveh. a foreign prophet says your city will be overthrown in forty days. what do you do?
o: rise from the throne, sit in ashes, and call the whole city to turn.
ignore it; prophets are always wrong.
games.why: the king leads the city in turning, and God sees their works and spares them.

practice: Think of someone you've written off, not someone dangerous, just someone you've decided is like that and always will be, and picture them a year from now, having changed one thing.
If you pray, you can pray for their turning and for your own patience; if not, simply leave the door open a crack.

wordCard.voice: Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, whose afternoon reading is Jonah, and a whole enemy city that turned.

orig.note: Hebrew: Nineveh, the capital of Assyria.

carryVoice: Your line: even Nineveh. What God saw was their works, not their sackcloth. See you tomorrow.
